paras: The attempted lynching of Lloyd Boyd took place at Annapolis, Maryland, in January 1903, when sailors and marines from the Naval Academy set out for the jail to lynch Boyd, a Black man held on a charge of shooting a navy sailor. Officers moved Boyd by train to the Baltimore city jail. The Baltimore Afro-American credited armed Black men who guarded the jail overnight and praised them in an editorial.

J. J. Kerns, a landsman on the torpedo boat destroyer Stewart, was shot in Annapolis on the night of Wednesday, January 14, and died at the Emergency Hospital; a coroner's inquest found death by shooting "by parties not yet determined." The next day police arrested two Black men, John E. Dryden, about forty, and Boyd, about fifty, and according to an Annapolis dispatch each said the other had fired. The Afro-American described Boyd as janitor of the Staunton Colored School and the dead man, whom it called Kearns, as a white seaman.

According to a Baltimore dispatch in the New York Sun, after Boyd was locked up "a large number" of sailors and marines scaled the academy walls and started for the jail to lynch him. A trunk of revolvers and dynamite was later found on College Avenue, and the dispatch reported a plan to blow up the jail unless Boyd was surrendered. At the suggestion of State's Attorney Daniel R. Randall, Sheriff N. C. Thomas Beasley and Deputy Sheriff Nicholas W. Bryan took Boyd from the jail at 12:40 a.m. and boarded a train for Baltimore.

The Afro-American told of a different defense of the jail. It reported that Black men, "fully armed," spent the night in a hall near the jail and patrolled the streets, while women of their families brought them coffee and sandwiches. In its account the authorities moved Boyd once they found that "the colored people of the city were determined that there should be no lynching." It added that St. John's College students climbed the college walls to join "the mob of sailors and others" but turned back.

The Sun reported that Boyd allegedly confessed on the train, saying "the devil got in him and made him shoot." The Afro-American instead said that an officer overheard Boyd talking with his attorney and repeated the "alleged confession" to the grand jury, which indicted him on it. No arrests of the would-be lynchers are reported, and no report of Boyd's trial or of Dryden's fate was found.

White coverage was brief. The Evening Star headed its arrest report "Two Negroes Accuse Each Other of the Crime," while the Sun ran the attempt under "SAILORS ON A LYNCHING BEE" and called Boyd "the colored murderer" of Kerns. The Sun told the story through the officers' actions and mentioned no Black response. Baltimore's German-language Deutsche Correspondent ran two short items, the second headed "Ein Lynchgericht befürchtet" ("A lynching feared").

A week later the Afro-American made the episode a story of Black self-defense under the headline "BRAVE BLACK MEN," and called the grand jury's use of the overheard confession "unheard of in the annals of criminal procedure." Its editorial commended the men for "the manly stand they took," said the unsafe jail could have "opened the way to another brutal lynching," and honored the women who supported them.

The Sun attributed Boyd's removal to the officers and the state's attorney, while the Afro-American credited the armed Black guard. The Sun's dispatch also places his arrival in Baltimore both "this afternoon" and after a 12:40 a.m. train, while the Afro-American and the Deutsche Correspondent date the removal to Saturday, January 17.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Lloyd Boyd
bases: Sailors and marines set out for the Annapolis jail to lynch Boyd, with a trunk of revolvers and dynamite and a threat to blow up the jail, and officers moved him to Baltimore for fear of lynching (A3, A4, A6); the lynching was attempted, not completed.

No one was killed: Boyd was removed to the Baltimore city jail (A3, A4, A6). A 'large number' of sailors and marines acted without authority on the accusation that Boyd shot a sailor (A3), so this is an attempted lynching.

A New York Sun dispatch (A3), the Baltimore Deutsche Correspondent (A4) and the Baltimore Afro-American (A5, A6) independently report that Boyd was moved to Baltimore because a lynching was feared; they differ on who deterred the mob.

accounts.label: Baltimore dispatch (officers' side)
accounts.gist: Sailors and marines scaled the academy walls to lynch Boyd, with revolvers and dynamite and a threat to blow up the jail; officers took him to Baltimore at the state's attorney's suggestion, and he allegedly confessed on the train.

accounts.label: Annapolis dispatch on the arrests
accounts.gist: Dryden and Boyd each said the other fired; the inquest named no one.

accounts.label: Black press (Afro-American)
accounts.gist: Armed Black men guarded the jail overnight and the authorities moved Boyd once they saw that the Black residents would not allow a lynching; the confession used before the grand jury was overheard from a talk with his attorney.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headed its arrest report 'Two Negroes Accuse Each Other of the Crime' and left the shooter undetermined.
The Sun headlined 'SAILORS ON A LYNCHING BEE' and 'Negro Murderer Hurried Out of Annapolis', treating Boyd's guilt as settled while reporting the mob's plan.
The German-language Correspondent ran two short local briefs, the second headed 'Ein Lynchgericht befürchtet'.
The Afro-American headlined 'BRAVE BLACK MEN', praised the armed defenders and their wives in an editorial, and attacked the grand jury's use of the overheard confession.

versions.value: Officers acted on the state's attorney's suggestion in the face of the sailors' threat
Authorities acted when they saw armed Black men would prevent a lynching

conflicts.note: The accounts are not exclusive; each reports only one side's role.

versions.value: taken from the jail at 12:40 a.m. by train

conflicts.note: The Sun dispatch is internally inconsistent; all place arrival in Baltimore on January 17.

conflicts.note: The Sun's confession is reported as 'alleged'; the Afro-American disputes how a confession reached the grand jury.

record_check.dossier: Shooting Wednesday Jan. 14; arrests Jan. 15; mob set out after Boyd was locked up and he was taken out at 12:40 a.m., arriving in Baltimore Saturday Jan. 17. The night of Jan. 16-17 is plausible for the attempt; 1903-01-17 is the dated removal.
